segments.t: At a celebratory drinks gathering, Mathias toasts his newly acknowledged family ties with Camille and Hippolyte. Over the table, Hippolyte unexpectedly offers to hire Camille as his exclusive talent agent, provoking a sharp clash with Mathias. Listen to the scene in French first.
À notre première réunion de famille!
Ça a du bon, de faire son coming out.
Camille, je crois en toi!
Je sais que tu en es capable.
Tu peux être un grand agent.
Je m'entends très bien avec Andréa.
Mes meilleures auditions, c'est grâce à toi.
Sans toi, je ne serais pas là.
Veux-tu être mon agent?
Hippolyte, tu as bu, calme-toi.
C'est mon premier verre, je suis sérieux!
Je ne sais pas, c'est trop vite.
Tu as des qualités, mais c'est trop tôt.
C'est dingue! Tu ne la soutiens pas.
Tu ne crois pas au talent de tes enfants!
Let's walk through the conversation step by step.
À notre première réunion de famille!
'To our first family get-together!' Raising a glass with 'to...' works just like in English, and 'family get-together' is built from 'reunion of family'.
Ça a du bon, de faire son coming out.
'There is a lot to be said for coming out.' Literally 'that has some good', this breezy idiom highlights a silver lining, borrowing English 'coming out' for revealing any secret.
Camille, je crois en toi!
'Camille, I believe in you!' When expressing deep faith in a person, French says 'believe in you' — matching English word-for-word.
Je sais que tu en es capable.
'I know that you have what it takes.' Because French says 'capable of something', 'of it' shrinks into a two-letter word tucked right before 'are'.
Tu peux être un grand agent.
'You can be a great agent.' Placed ahead of 'agent', this common word means 'great' in talent — whereas placed after, in French it would mean physically 'tall'!
Je m'entends très bien avec Andréa.
'I get on very well with Andrea.' Getting along with someone in French is literally 'hearing yourself well with' them — a handy expression for work or friendship.
Mes meilleures auditions, c'est grâce à toi.
'My best auditions are thanks to you.' Built around a cousin of English 'grace', 'thanks to you' in French is reserved strictly for positive outcomes rather than blame.
Sans toi, je ne serais pas là.
'Without you, I would not be here.' At the end, the short word that literally means 'there' is what you'll hear constantly in everyday French for 'here' as well.
Veux-tu être mon agent?
'Do you want to be my agent?' Inverting 'want-you' gives Hippolyte's offer a touch of earnest weight, and 'to be' follows 'want' directly in French.
Hippolyte, tu as bu, calme-toi.
'Hippolyte, you have been drinking, calm down.' Literally 'you have drunk', those three brisk words are how French speakers tactfully suggest someone is tipsy.
C'est mon premier verre, je suis sérieux!
'This is my first glass, I am serious!' One word in French covers both a drinking glass and a drink at a bar, so 'my first glass' means 'my first drink'.
Je ne sais pas, c'est trop vite.
'I do not know, this is too fast.' Pairing 'too' and 'fast' at the end gives a handy chunk whenever plans start moving faster than you expected.
Tu as des qualités, mais c'est trop tôt.
'You have qualities, but it is too soon.' Saying someone 'has some qualities' in French always means positive strengths, balanced here against 'too early'.
C'est dingue! Tu ne la soutiens pas.
'This is crazy! You do not support her.' Backing a person in French uses a cousin of 'sustain' — literally 'hold from underneath' — unlike the lookalike of 'support', which means 'tolerate'!
Tu ne crois pas au talent de tes enfants!

'You do not believe in your own children's talent!' Compare this with believing in a person earlier: before an idea like 'the talent', French switches from 'in' to 'to the'. Now let's listen to the whole dialogue again.
À notre première réunion de famille!
Ça a du bon, de faire son coming out.
Camille, je crois en toi!
Je sais que tu en es capable.
Tu peux être un grand agent.
Je m'entends très bien avec Andréa.
Mes meilleures auditions, c'est grâce à toi.
Sans toi, je ne serais pas là.
Veux-tu être mon agent?
Hippolyte, tu as bu, calme-toi.
C'est mon premier verre, je suis sérieux!
Je ne sais pas, c'est trop vite.
Tu as des qualités, mais c'est trop tôt.
C'est dingue! Tu ne la soutiens pas.
Tu ne crois pas au talent de tes enfants!
Hippolyte's sudden offer to Camille sparks family tension, revealing Mathias's reluctance to back his own children. See you next time!
À demain!
